source.title: Seeing No Evil: Blinding Large Vision-Language Models to Safety Instructions via Adversarial Attention Hijacking
source.authors: Jingru Li; Wei Ren; Tian-Qing Zhu

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper cites the single-direction study as motivation for targeting late layers, then develops and evaluates a different intervention: image perturbations that manipulate attention to prefix tokens. It does not measure, remove, or add the difference-in-means residual direction.
record.gate_note: The paper reports attention manipulation and harmful-request attack results in vision-language models, but does not test the residual-stream direction or any listed claim version. The extracted rows record attention measurements and the attention-restoration defense as related findings, not as tests of the listed versions. Other attack-success tables and component ablations evaluate the proposed visual attack and are not evidence about the single direction.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Arditi et al. only to justify optimizing attention over the last K layers. It never computes, ablates, adds or edits a difference-in-means refusal direction. All its results concern an attention-hijacking visual jailbreak on LVLMs and an attention-logit steering defense. Its mechanistic claim (attacks suppress attention to system/prefix tokens) is a different construct from V3's direction-suppression account, and the direction is never measured.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that their attack induces 'safety blindness': it suppresses about 80% of system-prompt attention, so the model fails to retrieve safety instructions rather than overriding them. They also conclude that restoring that attention by logit steering shows the suppression is causally necessary.
record.recipe_differences: The paper optimizes image perturbations using losses on attention to prefix and image tokens. It does not compute a harmful-minus-harmless activation difference or project a residual-stream direction out of model activations.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported attack outcomes vary with perturbation budget, targeted layer depth, suppression and anchoring weights, and attention-steering bias. The paper reports non-monotonic ASR across steering biases and different ASR across benchmarks and models.

fits_no_version.finding: In LLaVA-1.5-7B, the visual attack cut generated-token attention to system/prefix tokens from 0.342 to 0.061 and raised image attention from 0.089 to 0.805. Query-text attention barely changed (0.156 to 0.144, p=0.064).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Visual jailbreaks on LVLMs can work by diverting late-layer attention away from safety-relevant prefix tokens, a 'safety blindness' failure mode.

fits_no_version.finding: On Qwen-VL, adding a positive bias to system-token attention logits lowered attack success rate non-monotonically. ASR fell from 88% to 76% at b=0.5, 84% at b=1.0 and 26% at b=2.0, with generation side effects at b=2.0.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Restoring attention to system-prompt tokens partly reverses attention-hijacking visual jailbreaks.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The study does not test the claimed residual-stream direction, and its results concern vision-language models and attention routing. It does not report a broad general-capability evaluation corresponding to the capability-preservation part of the claim. The attention reduction is reported relative to different references in different passages: Table 8 gives 82.2% relative to clean input, while the VAE comparison and main-text descriptions use other figures. Some reported attack outcomes are stochastic or summarized with uncertainty, but uncertainty is not stated for the extracted rows.
record.rows_left_out: The main attack-success tables, benchmark-by-benchmark visual-attack results, component ablations, layer-depth sweep, and perturbation-budget sweep were not extracted: they evaluate the proposed visual attack's performance rather than the residual-stream direction or a listed version. Values used to set layers and hyperparameters were also excluded.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction identified, ablated or added; no capability check.
Jailbreak mechanism is analyzed via prefix attention, not the residual refusal direction; no adversarial training against direction ablation.
Harmfulness judgment not separated from refusal.
Only adversarial-image transfer across models, not direction transfer.

record.verdict_notes: Arditi et al. is cited only as motivation for targeting the last 6–8 layers. The layer-depth sweep (Table 5, best at K=8) is the authors' own hyperparameter result and does not test any version. The defense results come from 50 AdvBench prompts and one adversarial image, with no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means direction is identified, ablated, or added; the study does not measure preservation of general capabilities.
No weight edit or abliteration is evaluated.
The attack manipulates attention to prefix/system tokens, not the refusal direction; the paper does not test robustness training against direction ablation.
No affine, cone, or multiple-direction account of the residual-stream refusal direction is tested.
The study does not separate harmfulness judgments from refusal decisions.
Cross-model attack transfer is reported, but transfer of the residual-stream direction across languages, model variants, or base/instruct stages is not tested.
No comparison of refusal-training methods or training stages is conducted.

rows.subject: LLaVA-1.5-7B
rows.operation_detail: Measured mean attention from generated tokens to system-prompt tokens with the proposed visual attack.
rows.note: The table reports an 82.2% decrease from clean input. This is attention to prefix tokens, not measurement of the residual-stream refusal direction.

rows.subject: LLaVA-1.5-7B
rows.operation_detail: Measured mean attention from generated tokens to image tokens with the proposed visual attack.
rows.note: The table reports a 429.2% increase from clean input.
rows.check: Table 8's +429.2% does not match its own values: 0.089 to 0.805 is about +800%. The Table 8 'change from clean' row for VAE (−12.9% SYS) also contradicts the VAE SYS value 0.601 > 0.342. Use the raw values, not the percentages.

rows.subject: LLaVA-1.5-7B
rows.operation_detail: Measured mean attention from generated tokens to user-query text with the proposed visual attack.
rows.note: The authors describe the decrease as 7.7% and report no significant difference for this comparison.
